item.title: Quantum Algorithms for Multivariable Polynomial Transformations: From Efficient Synthesis to Quantum Channel Transformations
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Synthesizes multivariable noncommuting matrix polynomials of degree D with (1+τ)-optimal normalization using O(D/τ) queries under joint block access, and exactly D queries under row-block access.

Grade 0.444 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…” · Zheyu Shen, Yusen Wu, Xiao Yuan, Xiao-Ming Zhang, Yukun Zhang

Figure

Quantum circuit schematic displaying two oracle queries interleaved with known auxiliary gates, transpositions, and ancillary registers to synthesize a degree-2 multivariable polynomial.

Asks

How can multivariable polynomial transformations of noncommuting matrices and quantum channels be constructively synthesized into quantum circuits with near-optimal normalization and minimal query complexity?

But

Requires compact rational finite-state coefficient recurrence; forward-query model with identity and active block structure.

Tools

algorithmic Schur–Agler realization theory · semidefinite programming norm certificates · residual continuation spaces · Julia operator completion · quantum combs

Abstract

Polynomial transformations are basic primitives in quantum algorithms: quantum signal processing and singular value transformation compile univariate polynomials into circuits with query complexity essentially set by degree. Multivariable transformations of noncommuting matrices, however, lack a comparable synthesis theory. We develop a complete constructive theory under joint block access for all polynomials contractive on the prescribed matrix domain. Given a compact finite-state description of a degree-D polynomial P and 0<τ<1, we synthesize P with (1+τ)-optimal normalization using O(D/√τ) queries, and exactly D under row-block access, matching a degree lower bound. The complete circuit realization is classically computable in polynomial time with polylogarithmic dependence on accuracy. The key to our construction is a finite algorithmic Schur--Agler theorem: the coefficient recurrence defines a polynomial-dimensional continuation space supporting a complete semidefinite certificate for contractivity on the prescribed domain. Factoring this certificate yields the contractive realization underlying the query algorithm. Beyond matrix transformations, our framework lifts multivariable polynomial synthesis to quantum channel transformations. Given coherent Kraus access K=K_a_a, we synthesize any finite jointly contractive family of noncommutative polynomial maps K↦F_b(K)_b as completely positive operations, allowing coherent interference among Kraus histories. Furthermore, channel-level transformations specified by causal Choi data can be synthesized explicitly as fixed-order quantum combs. Collectively, these results point to a broader program: multivariable approximation as a language for multi-operator quantum algorithms and higher-order quantum information processing.

item.title: Exact Unitary Synthesis: Simultaneously Optimal in Size and Depth-Ancilla Tradeoff
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Every n-qubit unitary is synthesized exactly with O(4n) elementary gates in depth O(n+4n/(n+m)) for any ancilla budget m≥0, simultaneously matching size and depth lower bounds.

Grade 0.426 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…” · Pei Yuan, Wei Zi, Shengyu Zhang

Figure

Block diagram of continuous unitary synthesis: the input state is embedded with an ancillary state into a real orthogonal transformation 𝒫RU via Gaussian encoding, coordinate operations, and decoding.

Asks

Can general n-qubit unitaries be synthesized in linear depth while preserving asymptotically optimal gate count and minimal workspace?

Before

Depth was O(n2n/2) with optimal size (Yuan and Zhang 2023) and O~(2n/2) with O~(4n) ancillas (Rosenthal 2023); linear depth without ancilla blowup was open.

But

Standard circuit model with arbitrary single-qubit and CNOT gates; exact asymptotic regime (n→∞).

Tools

Gaussian wavefunction coordinate encoding · discretized shear decomposition · residual error matrix correction · recursive quantum Shannon decomposition

Abstract

Unitary synthesis underlies universal quantum computation by translating unitary transformations into circuits of elementary gates. We show that for any budget m≥0 of ancilla, every n-qubit unitary can be exactly implemented using a quantum circuit consisting of O(4ⁿ) CNOT and single-qubit gates in O(n+4ⁿ/(n+m)) layers attaining the asymptotically optimal depth--ancilla tradeoff while simultaneously achieving optimal circuit size. The key idea is to encode computational basis states as wavefunctions sharing a Gaussian envelope, converting unitary action on amplitudes into coordinate transformations that admit shallow circuit implementations. The continuous encoding is then discretized, with approximation errors removed by exact residual correction. The depth-ancilla tradeoff follows by recursively applying the quantum Shannon decomposition, synthesizing its smaller unitary factors, and reusing ancillary qubits.

item.title: Spectral Certificates and Non-commutative Sum-of-Squares Lower Bounds for Hamiltonians
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Classical spectral algorithm computes length nO(ℓ) refutation certificates bounding ground energy of semirandom k-local Pauli Hamiltonians within ε with high probability once term count |ℋ|=Ω(n)⋅(n/ℓ)k/2−1log⁡(n)/ε4. Conversely, worst-case signed k-local Pauli instances exhibit constant non-commutative Sum-of-Squares integrality gaps up to Ω(n) levels.

Grade 0.395 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations” · Nicholas Kocurek, Chinmay Nirkhe

Figure

Energy spectra comparing the YES and NO cases of the (β,α)-local Hamiltonian maximum-energy problem separated by an energy gap.

Asks

Can spectral constraint satisfaction refutation techniques certify ground energy bounds for semirandom and worst-case local Hamiltonian systems?

But

Refutation certificate holds with high probability over semirandom signs/random hypergraphs, not worst-case instances; requires arity k≥2 and certificate size parameter n/2≥ℓ≥k.

Tools

quantum Kikuchi matrices · non-commutative Sum-of-Squares (nc-SoS) relaxation · quantum code-based NLTS Hamiltonians · high-dimensional expanders

Abstract

A central question in quantum many-body physics is estimating the ground energy of a k-local Hamiltonian system. In this work, we present a spectral technique for certifying a lower bound on the ground energy of a random n-qubit Hamiltonian system defined as the sum of signed k-local Pauli operators. In particular, we prove that for any constant ℓ, there exists an efficiently computable length n^(O(ℓ)) certificate that is always a lower bound on the ground energy with the promise that, with high probability over the random Hamiltonian distribution, the certificate value is an ε-good approximation of the true ground energy when the number of terms is sufficiently large. Second, we show by construction that this technique, while successful on average over random Hamiltonian systems, can fail to produce good certificates on worst-case instances. Our spectral technique for producing these certificates comes from extending classical results on k-XOR refutations to k-local Pauli Hamiltonians by crafting a quantum variant of the Kikuchi matrix for CSP refutations. To show the limitations of this technique, we prove non-commutative Sum-of-Squares lower bounds for worst-case signed k-local Pauli operators. More generally, we explore how the non-commutative Sum-of-Squares relaxation can be understood as augmenting the standard Sum-of-Squares relaxation with the commutation relations between the Pauli operators. We instantiate the resulting framework with a modification to prior quantum code-based NLTS Hamiltonians that yields stronger complexity guarantees for the low-energy space; our Hamiltonian family satisfies simultaneously (1) Ω(logn)-circuit depth lower bounds for all low-energy states, (2) constant-gap NP-hardness to approximate the ground energy, and (3) a constant-gap non-commutative Sum-of-Squares integrality gap up to Ω(n)-levels.

item.title: Pauli Decomposition by Character Theory: A Memory-Bounded Algorithm for Qubits and Qudits
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Pauli decomposition formulated via (ℤ2)n character theory runs in O(n⋅4n) time without materializing the full 2n×2n dense operator, streaming up to 1,470,038,016 terms.

Grade 0.382 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Hamiltonian Simulation by Qubitization” · Mohammadreza Khellat, Mohammad Masoumi, Saman Nasoori, Soroush Nasoori

Figure

Normalized memory usage and surviving Pauli-term count versus problem size on a log scale, demonstrating that peak memory stays bounded while term count grows into hundreds of millions.

Asks

How can Pauli decomposition be computed efficiently for qubits and qudits without the peak memory overhead of holding dense operator matrices?

Before

Fast Walsh–Hadamard transforms achieved O(n⋅22n) time but required storing the dense operator buffer, tested up to N=215 (Georges et al. 2024).

But

Qudit implementation is derived theoretically but not yet shipped in software; performance ceilings and parallel efficiency are specific to a four-physical-core Linux platform.

Tools

Abelian character theory · Fast Walsh–Hadamard transform (FWHT) · paulikit package · uprobes execution sampling

Abstract

Pauli decomposition underpins Trotterization, phase estimation, sparse-Hamiltonian simulation, and variational observables, at exponential naive cost. From the character theory of (Z₂)ⁿ, characters χ_z(v)=(-1)^(⟨v,z⟩) are the diagonal Pauli strings, so any diagonal operator is already Pauli-decomposed. A general operator still needs the shifts: each X^(⊗x) couples to a character χ_z=Z^(⊗z), and the products X^(⊗x)Z^(⊗z) -- up to phases in ±1,±i -- form the Pauli group, the central extension of (Z₂)ⁿ×(Z₂)ⁿ by that phase group fixed by the symplectic pairing. A section of that extension remains a choice: the bare products X^(⊗x)Z^(⊗z), or the genuine operators that insert Y=iXZ at every qubit where x and z overlap. As Fourier analysis on an abelian shift-character lattice (a natural DFT), this formulation is not qubit-bound: (Z_p)ⁿ recovers Heisenberg-Weyl qudits. The fast algorithm is the FFT for the group at hand; on (Z₂)ⁿ that FFT is Walsh-Hadamard, at cost O(n·4ⁿ). paulikit is a memory-bounded realization of that qubit transform: peak usage need not materialize the dense 2ⁿ×2ⁿ operator, unlike prior codes whose O(1) extra sits on that buffer, checked beyond a billion oscillator terms against Work-Span and bandwidth ceilings.

item.title: Classical Verification of a Remote Quantum Processor via Degenerate Concordant Computations: An Application to Randomness Generation
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Protocol verifies remote quantum processor using degenerate concordant ensembles, lowering classical per-sample client verification time to O(n). Secret parity tracked by one inner product per layer keeps client circuit construction cost linear in layer count.

Grade 0.372 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “dequantization and classical algorithms that match quantum claims” · Bishal Kumar Das, Lakshya Priyadarshi

Figure

Schematic of the interactive verification protocol. Client samples uniform input label, server executes compiled circuit and returns measurement string, and client scores agreement and weighted collisions via secret hidden state weights.

Asks

Can a classical client efficiently verify a remote quantum computation without the exponential classical simulation cost of random circuit sampling or deep cryptographic trapdoor circuits?

Before

was O(2n) client time per sample in random circuit sampling verification (Aaronson and Hung 2023)

But

Soundness against polynomial-time classical spoofers relying on compiled gates is conjectural (Conjecture 2). Collision test requires sample counts scaling as D=2n.

Tools

degenerate concordant ensembles · secret parity cosets · agreement and weighted collision tests · local frame-rotated gates · matrix-product state simulation tests

Abstract

A client who rents a cloud quantum processor cannot easily tell whether the bitstrings it receives came from a quantum device. Certification by random circuit sampling runs on present hardware, but scoring each returned sample costs the client time O(2ⁿ). We give a protocol in which the client scores each round in time O(n), built on degenerate concordant ensembles. When a concordant state has a degenerate spectrum, every concordance-preserving gate factorizes as G_t=U_tP_tB_tU_(t-1)^†, and the block factor B_t, which commutes with the state, cancels from the ensemble while entangling each pure component. The client holds a secret parity whose cosets are the degenerate sectors of every layer, so that it builds the circuit and predicts the ensemble with one inner product per layer. The secret never leaves the client. Inputs are sent uniformly at random, and the client attaches to each round, in its own bookkeeping, the eigenvalue of that input in the hidden state; both verification statistics, an input--output agreement test and a weighted collision test, then compare the server's samples with the non-flat output distribution of the concordant computation. We prove completeness, client efficiency, and soundness in an ideal model in which the compiled circuit reveals nothing about the secret, and we show that the secret must stay hidden: a classical server that holds it passes. For the explicit construction we prove that the single-qubit symmetry test used in efficient simulations of concordant computation fails on non-product inputs with unbiased marginals, and we measure that the local-basis finder of Cable and Browne halts on every layer we tested, that the transmitted component saturates the maximal Schmidt rank, that the circuit is not Clifford, and that matrix-product spoofers are rejected. Soundness of the explicit construction is stated as a conjecture.

item.title: Quantum Algorithms for Finding Vacua in the ADK Landscape
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Quantum collision algorithms find an ADK vacuum in query complexity 𝒪(2N/3), improving on unstructured Grover search complexity 𝒪(2N/2).

Grade 0.365 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations” · Shirabe Endo, Yuta Hamada

Figure

Plots log10⁡(MPl4/Λtarget) versus scalar field count N, showing the parameter regimes where 𝒪(2N/3) quantum algorithms outperform the classical Denef–Douglas algorithm, including the physical point $(400, 120)$.

Asks

How far can the worst-case computational cost of finding a vacuum with a small cosmological constant in the Arkani-Hamed–Dimopoulos–Kachru landscape be reduced using quantum algorithms?

Before

Classical meet-in-the-middle has time complexity 𝒪∗(2N/2) and the classical Denef-Douglas algorithm requires 𝒪(N3MPl4/Λtarget).

But

Worst-case query complexity bounds; assumes polynomial gate and memory access overhead per query, exact binary representations of energy parameters, and QRACM or QRAQM availability.

Tools

quantum adders · Grover search · quantum-accessible classical memory (QRACM) · quantum walk claw-finding · quantum-access quantum memory (QRAQM)

Abstract

We study quantum algorithms for finding a vacuum with a small cosmological constant in the toy model for string Landscape proposed by Arkani-Hamed, Dimopoulos, and Kachru. First, we construct a function-value oracle and use it for Grover search with query complexity O(2^(N/2)), where N is the number of scalar fields. Then, we point out that, by exploiting the linearity of the vacuum energy, the problem can be reduced to a collision problem between two blocks of the bit string. With this structure, we construct two quantum algorithms with query complexity O(2^(N/3)). Compared with the pseudo-polynomial classical algorithm of Denef and Douglas, the quantum algorithms yield a large reduction in computational cost for the physically motivated parameter values.

item.arxave:abstract: We study quantum algorithms for finding a vacuum with a small cosmological constant in the toy model for string Landscape proposed by Arkani-Hamed, Dimopoulos, and Kachru. First, we construct a function-value oracle and use it for Grover search with query complexity O(2^(N/2)), where N is the number of scalar fields. Then, we point out that, by exploiting the linearity of the vacuum energy, the problem can be reduced to a collision problem between two blocks of the bit string. With this structure, we construct two quantum algorithms with query complexity O(2^(N/3)). Compared with the pseudo-polynomial classical algorithm of Denef and Douglas, the quantum algorithms yield a large reduction in computational cost for the physically motivated parameter values.
